items.title: Fake QR Codes on Parking Meters Are Stealing Card Numbers — FTC Warns
items.summary: The FTC is warning about fake QR codes — the square black-and-white patterns you scan to pay for parking. Scammers print their own codes and stick them over the real ones on parking meters. Scan the wrong one and it opens a fake payment page that steals your card number. Before you pay, check the code: if it looks like a sticker slapped over the real sign, don't scan it. Type the parking service's web address yourself, pay at the machine, and report fakes at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

items.title: Windows 11's Smart App Control stops bad apps before they run — turn it on free in Windows Security
items.summary: Windows 11's Smart App Control checks every program before it opens and blocks the ones that look untrusted — and it's free, built right into Windows. Most computers just have it sitting there, turned off. To switch it on, open the Windows Security app that came with your computer, go to App & browser control, and turn on Smart App Control. It's about one click and it's from Microsoft. If your computer doesn't show the option, that's normal on some machines — bring it by and I'll set up the next-best protection for you.

items.title: That slow old laptop isn't done yet — ChromeOS Flex is Google's free operating system that makes it fast again
items.summary: ChromeOS Flex is Google's free operating system built for older computers, and it can help a slow old laptop feel quick again. It's free at chromeos.google/products/chromeos-flex — Google gives you the download and the steps to put it on a USB stick, and the laptop starts up from that stick. If that sounds like more than you want to tackle, that's exactly what I'm here for.

items.title: Fake Car-Dealership Websites Are Taking Deposits — FTC Warns
items.summary: The Federal Trade Commission is warning about scammers cloning real car-dealership websites. They copy the logo, car photos, and customer reviews, then take an upfront deposit for a vehicle that doesn't exist. Buyers show up at the lot and find no record of their order or money. Before paying: search the dealer's name plus the word "scam," and insist on seeing the car in person or having an independent inspector check it. Never send a deposit by wire transfer. Report fake dealer sites at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. (Source: FTC, Sept. 1, 2026)

items.title: The Windows 11 September update finally brings back the movable taskbar — put it back at the top in Settings, free from Microsoft
items.summary: Microsoft's September update for Windows 11 is rolling out now, and it brings back the choice owners have asked for since 2021: you can move the taskbar back to the top of the screen or to either side. Check for the update at Settings → Windows Update, then open Settings → Personalization → Taskbar → Taskbar behaviors and pick where you want it. It's free, built into Windows, and takes about a minute once the update is installed.

items.title: Is your flash drive crawling? Plug it into the blue USB port — it's many times faster and it's already on your computer
items.summary: Look at the USB ports on your computer: some are black, some are blue. The blue ones are the fast kind — a flash drive or camera card reader can run many times quicker in them than in the old black ports. There's no software to download and nothing to install — just move the plug. If you don't have blue ports, the black ones still work fine; they're just slower.

items.title: FBI Warning: One Click Can Hand Scammers Your Email — No Password Needed
items.summary: The FBI put out a warning yesterday about a new trick: scammers send you a link that opens a real-looking Google or Microsoft screen asking, "Allow this app access?" One click hands them your email — your messages, your contacts, your password-reset emails — even though your password never changed, and even with two-step sign-in on. Change your password afterward and they still stay logged in. Fix in two minutes: open your email account settings and look for "connected apps" or "third-party access," then remove anything you don't recognize. Never approve an access request you didn't start. (Source: According to the FBI's official Internet Crime Complaint Center, September 1, 2026)

items.title: Google's free Security Checkup shows every device signed into your Gmail — run it in 2 minutes at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup
items.summary: Run Google's free Security Checkup at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup. It lists every device signed into your Gmail and lets you sign out any device you don't recognize — it takes 2 minutes and Google walks you through it step by step.

items.title: Copy text out of any screenshot — the Windows Snipping Tool's Text Actions does it in one click
items.summary: The Snipping Tool that's already on your Windows 11 computer can pull the words out of any screenshot. Press the Windows key + Shift + S to take a snip, click the Text Actions button at the top of the picture, then click Copy — now the words paste like normal text. Built into Windows, free, no download.

items.title: Fake Chrome Update Pop-Ups Are Spreading Malware
items.summary: Security writers are warning about fake browser-update pop-ups: a notice claiming your browser needs a "critical update." Clicking it installs malware, not an update. Real updates come from the browser's own menu — never from a website pop-up. If you see one, close the tab without clicking, then update properly: in Chrome, click the three dots, choose **Help → About Google Chrome**, and let it update itself. Then check your extensions and remove anything you don't recognize.

items.title: 300+ malicious Chrome extensions caught leaking browser data — audit yours in Chrome's Extensions manager
items.summary: Security researchers found more than 300 malicious Chrome extensions collecting browsing history or stealing user information. Open Chrome, click the three dots, choose **Extensions → Manage Extensions**, and remove anything you don't recognize or no longer use.

items.title: Audit your Chrome extensions in two minutes — Manage Extensions finds the fakes
items.summary: In Chrome, click the three dots, choose **Extensions → Manage Extensions**, and turn off anything you don't recognize or no longer use — one at a time, so you'll know what changed. Real updates come from the browser's own menu, never from a website pop-up.
